strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: reconstructing objects when the manipulating hand obscures precisely the geometry needed for interaction. Combining visual priors with known hand geometry and tactile contacts is well motivated.

The proposed integration is technically coherent. A shared camera-aligned SDF representation supports multimodal conditioning, differentiable contact and penetration losses, and guidance during generative sampling. Compatibility with downstream refinement pipelines adds practical value.

The reported simulation results suggest meaningful improvements under severe occlusion. In Table 1, B5 voxel IoU improves from SAM3D’s 0.337 to 0.532 and CD decreases from 0.153 to 0.109. Table 2 also reports substantial pose improvements, including against SAM3D supplied with ground-truth depth.

Experiments on a real humanoid with an unseen hand provide useful preliminary transfer evidence. The paper appropriately acknowledges calibration sensitivity, limited grid resolution, and the limits of cross-embodiment generalization, while attributing its principal architectural and dataset foundations.
weaknesses: The central physical-grounding contribution is not adequately isolated or measured. There are no controlled ablations separating physical training losses from inference guidance, or contact consistency from non-interpenetration. Nor are penetration volume, contact error, or physical-violation rates reported. Reconstruction metrics and selected visualizations cannot establish how much the proposed constraints improve physical feasibility, including after Stage B refinement.

The sensing ablation contains substantive numerical inconsistencies. In Table A1, No-Touch aggregate NC is 0.760, below every bin value (0.803–0.868), and aggregate voxel IoU is 0.430, also below every bin value (0.526–0.616); neither can be an ordinary weighted average over those bins. Moreover, all per-bin NC, F-score, IoU, and EMD values exactly match the full model in Table 1, despite differing aggregate values. These issues directly undermine the evidence for the claimed benefit of touch and require corrected results and an explicit aggregation protocol.

The metric-scale evaluation protocol is insufficiently specified. Appendix A.2 constructs the simulation grid by jointly fitting the ground-truth object and hand, whereas real inference uses a different image-mask-based procedure. The paper needs to establish whether simulation test preprocessing uses unavailable object geometry and how the grid-to-metric transform is recovered at inference. Alignment, normalization, metric units, and real-world ground-truth registration are also unclear, making the shape and pose comparisons difficult to interpret.

Experimental reporting limits confidence in the comparisons. Section 4.1 reports 36 test objects and 22,680 images, whereas Appendix A.2 lists 35 objects and 20,760 images. Only valid output meshes are evaluated, without failure rates or confirmation of a common evaluation subset. The real experiment covers five objects but omits trial counts and uncertainty estimates. The claim of improvement on all reconstruction metrics except the least-occluded F-score is also overstated: SAM3D has higher F-score in B1–B3 and overall, and better real-world EMD.

Reproducibility is limited by missing implementation details: latent dimensions and network sizes, optimization settings and training duration, loss weights and warmup, sampling steps, guidance coefficients, and the precise stabilization/projection rules. It is also unclear which refinement configuration produces the quantitative results. Runtime and memory measurements would help assess the practical cost of decoder-based gradient guidance.

The originality lies primarily in integrating established SDF, flow-matching, multimodal-conditioning, and geometric-constraint components. That integration could support acceptance, but comparisons are confined to vision-only external baselines and the problematic sensing ablation. An equal-input alternative, such as applying contact and collision optimization to an existing reconstruction, would better establish the value of the proposed learned integration. Overall, the promising application and reported gains do not yet outweigh the unresolved validation and reporting concerns.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: recovering object geometry under severe hand occlusion while preserving metric scale and compatibility with observed contacts. Combining visual priors with known hand geometry and tactile observations is well motivated.

The method forms a coherent pipeline: camera-aligned SDFs provide a shared representation for multimodal conditioning, contact losses, non-interpenetration losses, and differentiable sampling guidance. The paper appropriately attributes its underlying generative models and datasets.

The reported results suggest useful improvements, particularly under heavy occlusion. In Table 1, B5 voxel IoU increases from SAM3D's 0.337 to 0.532, and CD decreases from 0.153 to 0.109. Table 2 also reports improved pose metrics despite giving SAM3D ground-truth depth. Real-robot examples with an unseen hand provide encouraging feasibility evidence, and the limitations discussion candidly identifies calibration and resolution constraints.
weaknesses: The sensing ablation contains consequential numerical inconsistencies. In Table A1, every per-bin No-Touch entry for NC, F-score, voxel IoU, and EMD exactly matches the full model in Table 1, although the aggregate results differ substantially. Moreover, the No-Touch aggregate NC of 0.760 is below every bin value (0.803–0.868), and aggregate voxel IoU of 0.430 is below every bin value (0.526–0.616). These cannot be ordinary weighted averages over the reported bins. Corrected results are necessary to establish the contribution of touch.

The central contribution—physical constraints during training and sampling—is insufficiently isolated or directly evaluated. There are no controlled ablations separating conditioning, contact loss, non-interpenetration loss, and inference guidance, and no quantitative contact-error or penetration measurements. Figure A3 shows one guided trajectory without an unguided counterpart. Consequently, the evidence does not establish how much the proposed physical objectives contribute beyond supplying additional sensor information, or whether downstream mesh refinement preserves physical consistency.

The simulation protocol leaves a potentially important source of privileged information unresolved. Appendix A.2 constructs the grid by fitting and centering the known hand–object scene, while A.1 derives image placement from the posed object's grid bounding box. The real-world procedure instead uses hand geometry and image masks. The paper should establish whether simulated test preprocessing uses ground-truth object extent or pose unavailable at deployment, and demonstrate evaluation with the deployment-time procedure. This directly affects the metric-scale and pose claims.

Evaluation and implementation details are insufficient for reliable reproduction. The main text reports 36 objects and 22,680 test images, whereas Appendix A.2 reports 20,760 images. Invalid meshes are excluded without method-specific failure rates. Metric units, alignment and normalization conventions, real-world trial counts and ground-truth registration, and the evaluated Stage-B configuration are not adequately specified. Training schedules, major architecture settings, loss weights, guidance hyperparameters, and inference cost are also missing.

The conclusions overstate the consistency and breadth of the evidence. Table 1 shows lower F-score than SAM3D in B1–B3 and overall, rather than only in the least-occluded regime; real-world EMD and F-score also favor SAM3D. The real evaluation covers only five stated objects and does not report uncertainty or quantitative physical compatibility. These results support promising but mixed reconstruction performance and preliminary transfer, rather than the broader claim of reliably physically consistent reconstruction. Assessed as Algorithms/General, the useful integration does not yet have sufficiently dependable evidence for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: metric-scale object reconstruction when a manipulating hand obscures much of the object. Using proprioception as free-space evidence and touch as surface evidence is well motivated and relevant to robotic perception.

The method coherently combines camera-aligned SDF generation, volumetric hand/contact conditioning, and differentiable contact and non-interpenetration objectives. The shared geometric representation provides a practical interface to existing refinement pipelines. Under Algorithms/General, the main contribution is this integration rather than the individual established components.

The reported results show promising benefits under severe occlusion. In Table 1’s highest-occlusion bin, the method improves CD from SAM3D’s 0.153 to 0.109 and voxel IoU from 0.337 to 0.532. Table 2 also reports improvements in all pose metrics, despite supplying SAM3D with ground-truth depth.

Deployment on an unseen real robot hand is a useful feasibility demonstration. The paper appropriately acknowledges calibration sensitivity, limited grid resolution, and restrictions on cross-embodiment generalization, and attributes its principal architectural and dataset dependencies.
weaknesses: The sensing ablation contains consequential numerical inconsistencies. In Table A1, every No-Touch per-bin value for NC, F-score, voxel IoU, and EMD exactly matches the full model in Table 1, although their aggregate values differ substantially. Moreover, No-Touch’s aggregate NC of 0.760 is below every reported bin value (minimum 0.803), and its aggregate voxel IoU of 0.430 is below every bin value (minimum 0.526). These cannot be ordinary weighted averages over the stated bins. Corrected results are essential because this ablation is the main evidence isolating touch’s contribution.

Physical consistency is central to the contribution but is not evaluated directly with penetration volume/depth, contact-to-surface error, or constraint-satisfaction rates. There are also no controlled ablations separating physical training losses from inference guidance, or contact loss from non-interpenetration loss. Figure A3 illustrates a sampling trajectory but does not establish improvement over unguided sampling. It is therefore unclear how much benefit comes from the proposed physical objectives beyond additional sensor information, and whether refinement preserves those constraints.

The simulation protocol leaves possible access to ground-truth geometry unresolved. Appendix A.2 normalizes and centers the combined hand–object geometry, while A.1 derives image placement from the posed object’s grid bounding box. The manuscript should establish whether test-time preprocessing uses ground-truth object extent or pose, and whether every method receives equivalent information. The real-world hand/mask-based procedure differs and is insufficiently specified to resolve this concern. This matters particularly for the metric-scale and pose claims.

Evaluation details are insufficient for interpreting or reproducing the comparisons: metric units and normalization, alignment procedures, surface sampling, the definition of occlusion, and invalid-output counts are not adequately specified. Evaluating only valid meshes may bias comparisons without per-method failure rates. The main text reports 36 objects and 22,680 test images, whereas Appendix A.2 lists 35 objects and 20,760 images. Essential training settings, loss weights, guidance parameters, and inference runtime are also missing.

The real-world evidence is limited to five stated objects, without trial/image counts, uncertainty estimates, or a clear ground-truth registration protocol. It supports feasibility but provides limited evidence for broad robustness or generalization. The reported metrics are mixed: the method improves voxel IoU but trails SAM3D on F-score and EMD.

Some performance claims overstate the tables. Section 4.2 suggests F-score is worse only in the least-occluded regime, but it is worse in B1–B3 and overall (0.189 versus 0.228). This is a correctable presentation issue; the more substantive concerns are the inconsistent ablation and missing validation of physical consistency. Together, these prevent the otherwise promising contribution from supporting acceptance in its current form.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: metric-scale amodal reconstruction during manipulation, when hand occlusion makes visual inference unreliable. Under Algorithms/General, the main contribution is a coherent integration of generative shape priors, proprioception, and tactile constraints.

The shared camera-aligned SDF representation makes contact consistency and non-interpenetration differentiable and supports both training losses and inference guidance. The formulation is technically motivated, and the manuscript appropriately attributes its underlying generative architectures and representations.

Simulation results show meaningful improvements, particularly under severe occlusion. In Table 1, the highest-occlusion bin improves voxel IoU from SAM3D’s 0.337 to 0.532 and reduces CD from 0.153 to 0.109. Table 2 also reports consistent pose improvements, even when SAM3D receives ground-truth depth.

Table 4 provides useful evidence beyond comparisons with methods receiving different inputs. Modality ablations support complementary benefits from proprioception and touch, while component ablations support the physics losses and combined tactile representation. Mask, calibration, and contact perturbations are also investigated.

Real-robot deployment and the supplementary DexYCB evaluation provide encouraging evidence of transfer to unseen hands. Table A1 reports substantially higher reconstruction coverage and lower intersection volume than the human-hand baselines. The limitations discussion candidly identifies calibration sensitivity and restricted geometric resolution.
weaknesses: The metric-scale evaluation protocol needs substantially clearer justification. Supplement A.3 constructs the simulated grid using both the ground-truth hand and object meshes, maximizing their joint extent and centering the scene in the image plane. A.2 also uses posed-object bounding-box metadata for image placement, whereas real inference uses a different, hand-and-mask-based procedure. The manuscript does not establish whether all simulated test preprocessing can be reproduced from the declared observations without privileged object geometry. Since scale and pose recovery are central claims, an evaluation using explicitly observation-only preprocessing is important.

Physical consistency is insufficiently measured in the main robotic experiments. Tables 1–4 report reconstruction and pose metrics but no contact residuals, penetration volume/depth, or physical violation rates. Table A1 provides intersection volume on DexYCB, which is useful but does not establish the separate effects of contact and non-interpenetration losses in the target setting. Reporting these quantities before and after guidance, and after Stage B, would directly test the principal contribution; refinement is not shown to preserve Stage A’s constraints.

Several evaluation details needed to interpret the results are absent: metric units and normalization, reconstruction alignment procedures, occlusion-bin counts, and how pose metrics are obtained from generated geometry. Section 4.1 excludes invalid meshes without reporting method-specific failure rates for the main experiments. The number of sampling seeds and uncertainty across objects or grasps are also unspecified; 22,680 rendered views are not equivalent to that many independent object-level tests.

The real-world evidence remains preliminary. Although five evaluation objects are listed, the number of trials, ground-truth registration procedure, and mask acquisition method are not described adequately. Cross-embodiment transfer and the simulation-to-real change occur together, as the supplement acknowledges. For DexYCB, the source or omission of tactile conditioning is unclear, making the otherwise promising comparison difficult to interpret fully.

Reproducibility is limited by missing implementation and training specifications, including latent dimensions, network configurations, optimization schedules, loss weights, and numerical guidance settings. The inference description also leaves unclear whether the decoder receives the noisy latent or a predicted clean latent and how the stabilization heuristics are applied. These choices materially affect the proposed mechanism.

The results discussion overstates superiority over SAM3D. Table 1 shows lower F@0.02 for the proposed method in B1–B3 and overall (0.189 versus 0.228), rather than only in the least-occluded regime. Real-world F-score and EMD also favor SAM3D. These tradeoffs do not invalidate the contribution, but they should temper claims of broadly higher reconstruction fidelity. The SAM3D B3 normal-consistency entry of 0.081 also appears inconsistent with neighboring values and warrants correction.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful computer-vision problem: metric-scale amodal reconstruction during manipulation, when hand occlusion makes visual inference ambiguous. Expressing visual evidence, hand geometry, and tactile contacts in a shared SDF domain is a coherent approach. I assess this as an Algorithms/General contribution.

The method combines a generative shape prior with explicit contact and non-interpenetration objectives during training and sampling. The formulation is understandable, and the integration with a downstream structured-latent reconstruction pipeline is practically useful.

Simulation results provide encouraging evidence. Compared with SAM3D, aggregate CD improves from 0.039 to 0.033 and voxel IoU from 0.504 to 0.586; the largest voxel-IoU advantage occurs under the heaviest occlusion. Table 2 also reports consistent pose-estimation improvements, even when SAM3D receives ground-truth depth.

Table 4 includes useful modality, noise, representation, and training/inference ablations. The progression from vision-only to proprioception and then touch supports the complementary value of the sensing modalities. Real-robot experiments and the supplementary DexYCB comparison provide additional transfer evidence; Table A1 reports substantially better F-scores and reconstruction coverage than the human-hand baselines.

The discussion candidly identifies calibration sensitivity and the loss of fine geometry caused by the shared 64-cubed grid. These are relevant limitations, and the corresponding noise experiments strengthen the assessment.
weaknesses: The principal claim of physical consistency is not directly evaluated in the main simulation and robot experiments. Tables 1–4 report shape and pose metrics, but not contact residuals, penetration volume, or physical-constraint satisfaction rates. Table A1 does include intersection volume on DexYCB, which is useful, but does not establish the effect of the physics losses or guidance on the target robotic setting. It is also unclear whether Stage B preserves the constraints enforced on Stage A. Physical metrics before and after refinement, including the corresponding ablations, are needed to substantiate the central claim.

The metric-scale evaluation protocol needs clarification. Supplement A.3 constructs the simulated grid by fitting the complete hand–object geometry, while A.2 uses pose-derived projected bounding boxes for conditioning-image placement. Real inference instead uses hand geometry and image masks. The manuscript does not establish that the simulated preprocessing can be reproduced without access to the unknown object geometry, or quantify the effect of this protocol difference. This is an unresolved source of privileged information, rather than demonstrated leakage, but it matters directly to the scale and pose claims.

Important evaluation details are missing: the coordinate units and normalization/alignment used for reconstruction metrics, real-world ground-truth registration, the number of real trials, and per-method invalid-mesh rates in the main experiments. Evaluating only valid meshes can change the comparison population. The supplementary DexYCB experiment also does not explain whether tactile conditioning is disabled or how contacts are obtained. These omissions make the reported comparisons difficult to audit.

The evidence supports a mixed accuracy tradeoff more clearly than the prose acknowledges. In Table 1, SAM3D has higher F@0.02 in B1–B3 and overall (0.228 versus 0.189), rather than only in the least-occluded regime as stated. On real data, SAM3D also has better F-score and EMD. These results do not invalidate the contribution, but they qualify claims of broadly improved geometric fidelity. The apparent SAM3D B3 normal-consistency error of 0.081 should also be corrected.

Reproducibility is limited by missing architecture dimensions, optimization schedules, training budgets, loss weights, and concrete guidance settings, including sampling steps and stabilization parameters. Quantitative results are said to average multiple seeds, but the seed count and variability are not reported. The many rendered test images arise from a small object collection and repeated grasps; per-object results or uncertainty estimates would better establish the robustness of the gains.

The novelty lies mainly in integrating established SDF, flow-matching, multimodal-conditioning, and geometric-guidance components. That integration can merit acceptance, but the present evidence does not sufficiently distinguish its benefit from simpler contact-constrained fitting or refinement using the same physical inputs. Together with the unresolved protocol and physical-validation issues, this leaves a slight preference for rejection despite the promising ablations and transfer results.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: metric-scale amodal reconstruction during manipulation, when hand occlusion makes visual evidence unreliable. Combining a generative shape prior with proprioception and tactile contacts is well motivated.

The method coherently integrates camera-aligned SDFs, volumetric contact conditioning, and differentiable contact/non-interpenetration objectives. Its contribution lies in this integration into occlusion-aware generative reconstruction rather than in new flow-matching machinery.

Simulation results are promising, especially under severe occlusion. In Table 1’s highest-occlusion bin, voxel IoU improves from SAM3D’s 0.337 to 0.532 and CD decreases from 0.153 to 0.109. Table 2 also reports consistent pose improvements against SAM3D supplied with ground-truth depth.

Table 4 provides useful sensing, noise, training-loss, and guidance ablations. Real-robot experiments and the supplementary DexYCB comparison broaden the evidence beyond synthetic reconstruction. The discussion appropriately acknowledges calibration sensitivity and limited grid resolution.
weaknesses: The metric-scale evaluation protocol needs clarification. Supplement A.3 canonicalizes simulated scenes using both ground-truth hand and object geometry, whereas A.4 describes a different, image-mask-based procedure for real inference. The manuscript does not establish whether simulated test preprocessing uses unavailable object extent information or how all methods receive equivalent normalization information. Metric units, alignment procedures, and threshold normalization are also insufficiently specified, making shape versus pose/scale improvements difficult to disentangle.

The central physical-consistency claim is incompletely evaluated. The main simulation and robot experiments report general reconstruction metrics but no contact residuals, penetration depths/volumes, or violation rates. Table A1 reports intersection volume on DexYCB, which is useful, but does not establish how training losses and sampling guidance affect physical validity on the principal benchmarks. It is also unclear whether Stage B preserves Stage A’s contact and non-interpenetration improvements.

The supplementary human-hand comparison leaves important input assumptions unresolved: it does not explain how tactile/contact conditioning is obtained on DexYCB, whether touch is disabled, or whether contacts are derived from annotated geometry. Precise supplied hand poses also differ from estimated-hand pipelines. These differences need explicit accounting before the comparison can establish the claimed advantage.

Reproducibility and experimental scope remain limited. Key architecture sizes, optimization schedules, loss weights, and guidance settings are not fully specified. The real-world evaluation covers five objects without reporting trial counts or uncertainty. Quantitative results average multiple seeds without specifying their number or variability, and the main benchmarks exclude invalid meshes without reporting method-specific failure rates.

Some conclusions overstate the reported results. Contrary to the text following Table 1, SAM3D has better F@0.02 in bins B1–B3 and overall, not only in the least-occluded regime; it also has better real-world F-score and EMD. The B3 SAM3D normal-consistency entry of 0.081 appears inconsistent and should be verified. These reporting issues are correctable, but the protocol and physical-validation gaps above leave a slight preference for rejection despite the promising contribution.
